sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: An upper level ridge over the area will shift inland today. Areas of fog will be the main concern across western Washington this morning. The next disturbance will move into the region this afternoon and will bring light lowland rain and mountain snow to the area. The pattern becomes more active next week as a series of systems brings widespread precipitation, gusty winds, and the increasing potential for coastal flooding.

sections.title: Short term (today through Monday)
paragraphs: An upper level ridge over the area this morning will push inland today, making way for the next system to move into the region by this afternoon and evening. Conditions are cool out there again this morning, with temperatures mainly trending in the upper 20s to mid 30s as of 1AM/09Z. Areas of fog have also redeveloped across the area again overnight, and with temperatures near freezing, can expect to see a few areas of freezing fog across the region again this morning.

An upper level low will then drop southward from the NE Pacific today and position itself offshore through Sunday. This system will bring the next round of light rain to the lowlands and light snow to the mountains. Rain will approach the coast by this afternoon and will then gradually push inland into the interior by this evening. Overall rainfall amounts will remain light through Sunday, with only a tenth to a quarter of an inch of rain expected along the coast and a few hundredths of an inch for the interior - with many spots remaining dry. Snow levels will hover between 2000-3000 ft, so will see some light snow accumulations (less than half an inch) at the Cascade passes. Afternoon high temperatures today and Sunday will be in the mid 40s to low 50s. Lastly, high astronomical tides over the weekend may bring the potential for some minor coastal flooding along the Pacific Coast and the Strait of Juan de Fuca by Sunday.

The low situated offshore will eventually become absorbed into the mean flow on Monday as a broad upper level low drops down into the NE Pacific from the Aleutians. Another round of precipitation will push inland, but will largely remain focused on the Olympic Peninsula. Snow amounts between 4-8 inches will be possible in the Olympics. Afternoon highs will be in mid 40s to low 50s.

sections.title: Long term (Monday night through Friday)
paragraphs: The aforementioned low will then deepen offshore Monday night into Tuesday and will bring a more active pattern to western Washington as the system swings a number of disturbances across the region. Expect multiple rounds of widespread lowland rain, mountain snow, and gusty winds starting Tuesday and persisting through the second half of the week. The system moving across the area on Tuesday will also bring another round of high surf to the coast. Additionally, high astronomical tides combined with the weather impacts from these systems, will increase the threat for coastal flooding - most notably along the Pacific Coast during high surf.

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Weak high pressure will begin to move out of the terminals today as an occluded front slows over water as it approaches the coastline. A column of low-end MVFR stratus has formed and work its way north through the Puget Sound this morning. Cameras however are showing fog and mist developing underneath the stratus layer, with much of it remaining localized over areas of water, and any low-lying areas or valleys. High cloud coverage does not arrive until early this afternoon, so this will likely keep lower ceilings/visibilities around through the morning - as late as 18Z. Showers with the front will arrive along the coast shortly after 18Z, and push inland towards 00Z. Overnight, as the showers push through ceilings will gradually lower to either a low-end VFR or MVFR level early Sunday morning, with the lowest ceilings in the south interior. Showers will continue Sunday with ceilings improving to VFR late in the morning. Winds will be out of the south/southeast 5-10 kt with a few gusts to 20 kt.

KSEA...Low MVFR ceilings likely to hang around the terminal through 18Z as high clouds arrive with the front. Cameras are picking up on lower areas of visibilities underneath the stratus near the terminal, particularly to the northeast (some patches of fog). VFR is expected after 18Z this afternoon with MVFR becoming likely post- showers overnight (as early as 09Z). Winds: southeast 5-10 kt with a few gusts to 20 kt later in the afternoon.
HPR

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: A front will slow to a near stall over the coastal waters this weekend, with high pressure moving out. Couple areas of fog may linger in the interior waters this morning. The front will bring some showers (no thunder expected through the weekend). Winds remain on track to increase with the frontal system this afternoon today into Sunday. This system will primarily affect the coastal waters, and the east Strait of Juan de Fuca, with winds of 20-30 kt today. The northwest coastal water zone does still have the best chance of a few gale gusts this afternoon. The coastal system will deepen and keep winds gusty on Sunday and into Monday out of the southeast. A couple strong system remains on track to impact the waters Monday into Tuesday, and Wednesday. PRobabilities remain high for gale gusts in the coastal waters, and a portion of the east Strait of Juan de Fuca. There remains a 20-40% chance of wind gusts reaching storm force criteria with of the next week systems.
Seas will build from 6 to 8 to 8 to 12 ft today, and continue to build on Monday up to 16 to 20 ft, before decreasing back to 10 to 14 ft by the end of next week.
HPR

sections.title: Hydrology
paragraphs: Wetter systems moving into the region next week will start to bring some rises to area rivers. At this time, no widespread river flooding is expected, however the Skokomish River will likely cross into flood stage late in the week.

discussions.name: NWS Portland
synopsis: Dry weather continues into Saturday morning before an active weather pattern returns. A series of Pacific frontal systems will bring multiple rounds of rain, mountain snow, and breezy winds starting midday Saturday and continuing through next week.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: Dry weather continues into Saturday morning before an active weather pattern returns. A series of Pacific frontal systems will bring multiple rounds of rain, mountain snow, and breezy winds starting midday Saturday and continuing through next week.

sections.title: Discussion
paragraphs: Now through Thursday...Visible satellite imagery early Friday afternoon depicts widespread stratus that had formed overnight slowly dissipating from southeast to northwest across NW OR and SW WA as weak, transient high pressure forms over the region. Stratus may not dissipate completely from far NW OR and SW WA before the sun sets, so these locations may end up with high temperatures a few degrees lower than forecast. Otherwise, high temperatures this afternoon one again are forecast to peak in the mid 40s across the Willamette Valley, 50s along the coast, and 30s along the Cascades. As the high pressure moves inland overnight, there's the potential for another round of fog/stratus forming tomorrow morning, though high clouds moving in ahead of the next weather system could limit that formation.

Today is the last dry day in the forecast through at least Thanksgiving Day. Multiple weather systems are slated to move through the PacNW through next week, bringing the return of a wet pattern. Precipitation returns Saturday as an upper level trough deepens in the eastern Pacific and pushes a frontal system inland tomorrow night into Sunday. Rain is forecast to begin along the coast by late Saturday morning, pushing inland as scattered showers over the afternoon, continuing into Sunday. Latest guidance indicates that the low will spin offshore through the day Sunday before moving northeast and weakening offshore of WA/BC on Monday. Because of this pattern of the low staying offshore, precipitation chances and amounts have decreased inland from yesterday's guidance, with higher precipitation chances of 70-95% over the Coast Range, Willapa Hills, and Coast. This has impacted the Cascade snow forecast, as well. Although snow levels will be around 2500-3500 ft, QPF amounts over these elevations will mainly be less than 0.1-0.25 inch. Therefore, the probability of snow amounts of at least 2 inches is now only 20-40% at pass level for Saturday through Sunday and less than 5% for 4 inches. For elevations higher than pass level, there's a 40-70% chance of at least 2 inches and 15-40% chance for at least 4 inches. Those who have outdoor plans over the high Cascades should still plan on snow covered roads at times, especially in stronger showers.

Ensemble guidance is in good agreement that another low pressure system will deepen in the eastern Pacific early next week, hot on the heels of the weekend system. Ensembles suggest this system will also spin offshore through much of the week, likely pushing multiple frontal systems inland through the week. The next frontal system bringing widespread rain and a period of breezy winds to the region will be late Monday into Wednesday. This system will have more Pacific moisture associated with it than the weekend system with latest ensembles indicating IVT values peaking around 500-750 kg/(ms). From late Monday through 4 AM PT on Thursday, there's a 60-80% chance of at least 1 inch of rain along the coast, 40-70% over the Cascades, and 25-60% for the inland valley, with highest probabilities around and north of the Columbia River. Looking at probabilities for at least 2 inches, those drop to 35-50% along the coast, 10-45% over the Cascades, and 5-20% for the inland valley. No significant flooding impacts are expected at this time, though periods of heavier rain could cause localized ponding of water in lower lying areas. Breezy winds are possible along the coast with the frontal passage on Tuesday, as well. There's a 40-65% chance of peak wind gusts at least 45 mph and a 5-20% chance for peak gusts at least 55 mph.

Beyond Wednesday, ensemble guidance becomes more uncertain on specific details of the low pressure system, though precipitation chances continue through at least Thanksgiving day. There is the indication that another frontal system may push into the region sometime Thursday into late week, causing another round of widespread rain and breezy winds. NBM has a 15-30% chance of peak wind gusts of 55 mph or higher on both Thursday and Friday with a 30-60% chance of at least 1 inch of rain across all of NW OR and SW WA for the 48 hour period ending at 4 AM PT Saturday. Keep an eye on the forecast, especially if you have travel plans for the upcoming holiday. -03

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Through 06Z Sunday...High pressure remains in place through tonight, bringing calm winds and the eventual development of fog and/or low stratus within the Willamette Valley with ceilings most likely ranging between 300-700 ft and increasing chances for surface visibilities below 1-2 SM. The main uncertainty is the exact timing of when fog and low stratus will redevelop and exactly when it will lift. Current guidance suggests fog and/or low stratus will redevelop sometime between 08-12Z Saturday, with 10Z being the most likely time. Most inland TAF sites should be impacted by fog or low stratus later tonight, except at KTTD.

A frontal boundary will push into the area from the southwest between 14-18Z Saturday, which will help lift lingering fog and low stratus to MVFR thresholds, and then to VFR thresholds. Rain showers will also be pushing into the area at that time.

KPDX AND APPROACHES...Mostly clear skies will most likely give way to either fog or low stratus sometime between 08-12Z Saturday, resulting in LIFR or IFR conditions. These conditions are expected to be relatively short-lived, as a frontal boundary will begin moving towards the terminal in the mid to late morning, bringing rain showers, rising ceilings, and improved surface visibilities. -23

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: Light southerly winds around 15 kt or less continue across the waters through this evening with seas around 5-6 ft at 11 seconds. The next frontal system arrives late tonight into Saturday, increasing southerly winds with gusts up to 30 kt. Small Craft Advisories are in effect tonight through early Sunday morning. For the outer waters beyond 10-20 NM offshore, isolated gale force wind gusts up to 35 kt are possible. Guidance did not suggest that gales would be frequent or widespread enough to warrant a Gale Warning. High confidence (70-90% chance) for seas building to 8-10 ft on Saturday, and 12-14 ft by Sunday.

Active weather continues next week as a series of systems impacts the waters. There is potential for storm force wind gusts early next week, with a 60-80% chance for at least isolated wind gusts exceeding 48 kt across the outer waters beyond 10 NM offshore. In addition, seas will also build into the mid to upper teens, with a 20-40% chance of exceeding 20 ft on Tuesday for areas beyond 30 NM offshore. For the Columbia River Bar, chances for seas exceeding 20 ft are currently around 5-15%.
Long period swells will also result in a moderate threat for sneaker waves through this weekend. Those visiting the coast should use extra precaution when in or near the water. -10
